prompt: Six services use a homegrown auth library with a known security weakness. You want all of them on the shared v2 library. You're a senior engineer on one of those teams, the other five have full quarters, and the document you sent to everyone produced two polite replies and a month of nothing. What now?
answer_markdown: Stop broadcasting and start talking to individuals — a document sent to six teams reliably generates polite silence, while six conversations generate two allies. Ask each team's engineers what would make this easy and what it collides with, and you will learn things the document could not surface: one team may already have an auth bug they cannot fix and would welcome the excuse to move, and another's service may be decommissioned in two quarters, making migration genuinely wasted work. Excluding that second team costs you nothing and buys enormous credibility, because it proves you care about the goal rather than about uniformity. Then do your own team plus the most-willing team first, write the migration guide from those two, and reduce every subsequent team's cost from 'two weeks of work' to 'review this PR'. Publish a tracker weekly — factual, no nagging — because nobody wants to be the last row. What you avoid is escalating early for a mandate, which produces minimal grudging compliance and burns the relationships you need next quarter.

prompt: Why is 'make participation cheap' more effective than making a better argument?
answer_markdown: Because you cannot make anyone do anything, so every team's participation has to be in their interest or at least cheaper than not participating — and being right about the architecture is not a force that moves people. A team with a full roadmap will decline a well-argued request for two weeks of work no matter how sound it is, because their constraint is capacity, not conviction. The same team will usually accept a pull request that needs twenty minutes of review. This reframes the whole problem from 'how do I convince them?' to 'what does this cost them, and can I reduce it?' The practical consequence is that writing the migration script, producing a codemod, or preparing another team's PR yourself is worth more than any number of meetings — and it is unglamorous work that is most of the job. It also explains why the effort estimate per team is the number worth attacking: cutting a team's cost from eight days to two does more for adoption than eight more conversations about why the migration matters.

prompt: Your cross-team migration is stalled at 70% and the remaining teams keep deprioritising it. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Change the defaults, because persuasion has already moved everyone it is going to move. Voluntary migrations reliably stall around this point — the remaining teams are the ones with the least pain and the most competing work, so more reminders produce nothing but irritation. Make the old way harder than the new way instead: have the project scaffolding generate the new service by default, add a deprecation warning on import of the old library, or put in a lint rule that blocks new usage. None of these forces anyone to migrate today, but they stop the problem growing and they shift the default. This is also the right moment for a different kind of escalation than the one people reach for at the start: not 'mandate this', but going to a director with 'four of six are done, the remaining two need about a week each — can it go on their Q3 plan?' That is easy to grant because you have already removed the risk and demonstrated it works, which is a completely different conversation from asking for a mandate on day one.

prompt: A team lead refuses to migrate. He has a customer commitment this quarter, he says the security weakness doesn't apply to his service — and he's technically right about that — and he's tired of platform work landing on his team. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Concede the technical point immediately and openly, which is both correct and disarming. Your goal was security, and insisting on migration here would mean you had quietly substituted tidiness for the actual objective — he knows his objection is sound, so pushing makes you the person who does not listen, and word of that travels to the other teams you still need. Then separate the two things bundled inside his no. The security case does not apply to him, fine. The maintenance case still does: the old library will be unowned, and in a year he will be the sole consumer of a dead dependency, which is his problem rather than yours. Offer a timeline that fits his constraint instead of yours — not this quarter, next, and you will write the PR. Also hear the real complaint, because 'platform work keeps landing on us' is a legitimate grievance about work allocation, and acknowledging it or raising it with his manager on his behalf buys more than winning would. If he still declines, accept it and keep him on the tracker with a note. Forcing a peer team is not available to you.

prompt: Four months into a migration you've driven, a newly hired staff engineer presents it at an all-hands as her workstream and doesn't mention you. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Go to her directly and privately with the offer rather than the grievance: here is the tracker, here are the two remaining teams, here is why each has stalled and the context on the lead who refused. If she now has the mandate and the resourcing, that is genuinely better for the outcome — you wanted the migration done, not credit for it, and it is 70% complete with a live security issue at stake. Publicly correcting the record makes you look territorial about something that was never yours to own, in front of everyone, and turns your closest ally on the one project you both care about into an adversary. Silent disengagement is worse, because it kills a migration that is nearly finished and leaves the risk live. Handle visibility separately and unemotionally: make sure your manager knows what you did, in writing, before performance review season. That is not politics, it is the documentation they need to advocate for you in a calibration meeting you will not attend. Interviewers use this scenario because it cleanly separates people motivated by the outcome from people motivated by ownership.

prompt: How do you get something onto another team's roadmap when you have no authority over them?
answer_markdown: Work their planning cycle rather than interrupting their quarter. A request that arrives mid-quarter competes against commitments already made and loses by default, whereas the same request made a few weeks before planning is just another candidate on the list. Three things make it competitive. Arrive with the cost already minimised — 'this is about two days, and I will write the migration script' is a different proposal from 'we need you to migrate'. Frame it in their pain, not yours, which means finding out what that pain is first: the problem you care about is often a symptom of one they care about more, and that reframing is worth more than any advocacy. And get a sponsor — a manager or staff engineer who will say 'yes, this matters' in the planning meeting you are not invited to. That is not politics, it is recognising that resourcing decisions happen in rooms you have no access to, and a written one-page document with options and a cost-per-team column is what circulates into those rooms when you are not there.
